demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
She is thirty-five, European, married, and works as a counselor in a community mental health clinic. Before the accident, she thinks of herself as careful with people and careful in general. She is the person who double-checks appointment times, who texts to make sure someone got home safely, who slows down in school zones even when no one is around. That image of herself splits sharply one rainy evening about a year ago.

She is driving home after a long day of back-to-back sessions. Her head is full of other people's stories, and she is already mentally sorting dinner plans with her husband. At an intersection near her neighborhood, she looks left, then forward, and begins a turn. A cyclist comes into view too late. She remembers the flash of a reflective jacket, the violent thud against the hood, and then a silence that feels impossible. When she gets out of the car, her legs shake so hard she has to hold the door. The cyclist is on the pavement, conscious but twisted in a way that tells her immediately this is serious. She kneels beside him in the rain, talking too fast, hearing her own voice become thin and unreal. Someone else calls emergency services. She keeps saying, "I'm so sorry," while blood mixes with water on the road.

At the hospital she learns he has survived but has multiple fractures and a head injury. No alcohol, no speeding, no criminal charge-an accident. Friends and family repeat that word to her as if it should settle something. It does not. She hears "accident" and thinks, I still did it. In the first weeks, she barely sleeps. Each time she closes her eyes she sees the cyclist rising into her headlights again. Sometimes the image is exactly as it happened; sometimes it is worse, with details her mind supplies in merciless slow motion. She wakes with her heart pounding, grabbing at the sheets, already apologizing aloud. Her husband reaches for her and she stiffens before she realizes where she is.

Driving becomes an ordeal almost immediately. She starts avoiding that intersection, then the whole route, then driving altogether if she can help it. On days she has to go to work, she leaves absurdly early so she can take side streets and stop to steady her breathing when her hands begin to sweat on the steering wheel. If a pedestrian steps off a curb, even far away, she feels a jolt through her chest. She scans constantly for cyclists, dogs, children, anything that might dart into the road. By the time she reaches the clinic, she is exhausted.

At work, the change is harder to hide than she wants to admit. She has spent years sitting with other people's guilt and grief, helping them name what happened without being consumed by it. Now when a client mentions a car accident, emergency sirens, or harming someone unintentionally, she feels her concentration fragment. She nods, but part of her is back in the rain, staring at the pavement. She starts rearranging her caseload when she can, trading clients whose stories come too close to her own. After sessions she sits in her office with the door locked, ashamed that she cannot do the one thing she asks of others: stay present.

She also begins to punish herself in small, private ways. She stops listening to music in the car because she no longer feels she deserves comfort. She avoids meeting friends who ask casual questions like, "How are you doing?" because she cannot bear either their sympathy or their attempts to reassure her. When her husband suggests a weekend trip, she refuses; the thought of unfamiliar roads makes her nauseated. Their world gets smaller. He notices that she startles when he enters a room unexpectedly and that she is checking the front window at night as if someone might come to accuse her. She has looked up the injured man online more than once, searching for updates, half hoping for evidence that he has recovered and half fearing what she might find. She has written him letters she never sends.

What disturbs her most is the shift in how she understands herself. She used to trust her own judgment. Now she replays ordinary decisions for signs of hidden recklessness: Did I look carefully enough? Was I tired? Was I distracted by my own life while someone else paid the price? She knows, intellectually, that a moment can be tragic without being malicious. But in the quieter hours of the evening, intellect gives way to something harsher. She sits at the kitchen table long after dinner, hearing again the sound of impact, feeling the cold rain on her coat, and thinking that the worst thing she has ever witnessed is also the worst thing she has ever done.

Months later, the cyclist is alive, and everyone around her marks that fact as the ending. For her, it is not an ending at all. The event continues to live in her body and in the narrowed shape of her days. She still drives only when she must. She still wakes before dawn from dreams in which she reaches the intersection over and over and never manages to stop in time. And each morning, before she opens her office door to welcome the first client, she pauses with her hand on the knob, gathering herself against the fear that one ordinary lapse can undo an entire life.
